demo.welcome_caption: Explore how large language models work: from text to tokens, attention, training and retrieval.
demo.welcome_say: Welcome to NeuroGraph X R. In this short tour, you will see how large language models work, from tokens and attention, to training and retrieval.

category_say.Data & Tokens: Everything starts with data and tokens: the training text, and the tokenizer that cuts it into pieces.
category_say.Representation: Tokens become numbers. Embeddings and position information tell the model what each token means and where it sits.
category_say.Architecture: The architecture: attention, feed forward layers and residual connections form the Transformer.
category_say.Training: Training: pretraining on huge data, then fine tuning and alignment with human preferences.
category_say.Generation: Generation: after training, the model picks one token at a time, using decoding rules like temperature.
category_say.Retrieval: Retrieval: R A G adds outside knowledge by searching documents before the model answers.
category_say.Evaluation: Evaluation: benchmarks and metrics tell us how good a model really is.

story.title: The big idea: predict the next word
story.caption: An LLM does one simple thing: it predicts the next word.  "The cat sat on the ..."  ->  "mat".  Everything else is machinery to do this well.
story.say: A large language model does one simple thing. It predicts the next word. Given the cat sat on the, it predicts mat. Everything you will see now is machinery that makes this prediction good.

story.title: Step 1: it learns from text
story.caption: Garbage in, garbage out: the model is only as good as its data. Missing languages or topics make it weak there (data bias).
story.say: First, the model learns from a huge amount of text, called Training Data. Garbage in, garbage out. If some languages or topics are missing, the model is weak there. This problem is called Data Bias.

story.title: Step 2: text becomes tokens
story.caption: "Hello world!"  ->  [Hello] [ world] [!]  ->  one ID number per piece. Computers only understand numbers.   (Press L to try your own text in the Token Lab.)
story.say: Computers only understand numbers, so text is cut into small pieces by the Tokenizer. A common method is Byte-Pair Encoding, which merges frequent letter pairs into bigger pieces. Special Tokens mark things like the start or the end.

story.title: Step 3: tokens become meaning
story.caption: ID numbers are arbitrary. An embedding turns each token into a list of numbers where similar meanings sit close together.
story.say: But ID numbers carry no meaning. So each token is looked up in the Embedding Matrix, and becomes a list of numbers, called an Embedding. Similar meanings get similar numbers, and Cosine Similarity measures how close two meanings are.

story.title: Step 4: the order of words
story.caption: "Dog bites man" is not "man bites dog". The model must know each token's position.
story.say: Order matters. Dog bites man is not the same as man bites dog. Positional Encoding adds the position of every token, and RoPE is the modern way to do it.

story.title: Step 5: why attention was invented
story.caption: Old models squeezed a whole sentence into ONE vector and forgot details. Attention lets the model look back at every word.
story.say: Early models, called Encoder-Decoder models, squeezed a whole sentence into one single vector. This Information Bottleneck lost detail in long sentences. Attention fixed it, by letting the model look back at every word.

story.title: Step 6: how attention works
story.caption: Like a library: the QUERY is what you look for, the KEY is each book's index card, the VALUE is the book's content.
story.say: Think of a library. In Query, Key, Value attention, the query is what you look for, the key is the index card of each book, and the value is the book itself. In Self-Attention, every token asks which other tokens matter. Masked Attention hides the future words, and Multi-Head Attention looks from several viewpoints at once.

story.title: Step 7: the Transformer
story.caption: Attention + feed-forward network + skip connections = one Transformer block. Stack many blocks = a large language model.
story.say: Combine attention with a Feed-Forward Network and Residual connections, and you get a Transformer block. Stack many of these blocks and you have a Large Language Model. Later you will see inside one block.

story.title: Step 8: how it is trained
story.caption: Predict the next token, billions of times, in batches on GPUs. Scaling laws: more data and compute give predictably better models.
story.say: Now training. In Pretraining, the model reads enormous amounts of text and predicts the next token, billions of times. This runs in Batching, on GPU Compute, which are graphics processors that multiply huge matrices. Scaling Laws show that more data and more compute make the model better in a predictable way.

story.title: Step 9: teaching it to be helpful
story.caption: A pretrained model knows language but does not follow instructions. Fine-tuning on good answers and human preferences fixes that.
story.say: After pretraining, the model knows language, but it does not yet follow instructions. Supervised Fine-Tuning teaches it from example answers. RLHF uses human preferences, and DPO is a simpler way to learn from them. Together, this is called Alignment.

story.title: Step 10: generating text
story.caption: The model predicts one token, adds it to the text, and repeats. Decoding is the rule that picks the token.
story.say: To write text, the model predicts one token, adds it to the text, and repeats. This is called Inference. Decoding is the rule that picks the next token. Greedy Decoding always takes the most likely one.

story.title: Step 11: temperature
story.caption: Temperature controls how adventurous the choice is. Watch how the probabilities change.
story.say: Temperature controls how adventurous the model is. Watch how the probabilities for the next word change. Top-k and Top-p sampling also limit the choices to the most likely words.

story.title: Step 12: adding your own knowledge (RAG)
story.caption: A model only knows its training data and may invent answers. RAG first searches your documents, then answers from what it found.
story.say: A model only knows its training data, and it can invent answers. Retrieval-Augmented Generation, called RAG, fixes this. Chunking splits your documents into pieces. Embedding Models turn the pieces into numbers. A Vector Store finds the closest pieces to the question, and the model answers from them. This reduces Hallucination.

demo.question: How does RAG reduce hallucination?
demo.tour_end: Tour finished. From text and tokens through the Transformer to training, generation and retrieval: that is how an LLM system works.
demo.summary: Tokens, embeddings, attention, the Transformer, training, decoding and RAG. Press D to replay, or Q for the quiz.

nodes.label: Training Data
nodes.desc: Huge text collections from the web, books and code that a language model learns from.

nodes.label: FineWeb
nodes.desc: A large cleaned web dataset built by filtering, removing duplicates and scoring the quality of crawled pages.

nodes.label: Data Bias
nodes.desc: Models inherit the imbalances of their data, for example favouring English over other languages.

nodes.label: Tokenizer
nodes.desc: Splits text into tokens and maps them to integer IDs before the model sees anything.

nodes.label: Byte-Pair Encoding
nodes.desc: Builds a vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent pairs of symbols.

nodes.label: Special Tokens
nodes.desc: Reserved tokens that mark things like the start, the end, or the roles in a chat.

nodes.label: Context Window
nodes.desc: The maximum number of tokens the model can read and write in one go.

nodes.label: Embedding Matrix
nodes.desc: A lookup table with one learned vector for every token ID.

nodes.label: Embeddings
nodes.desc: Dense vectors of numbers in which tokens with similar meaning lie close together.

nodes.label: Cosine Similarity
nodes.desc: Measures how similar two vectors are by the angle between them.

nodes.label: Word2Vec
nodes.desc: An early method that learns word vectors by predicting a word from its neighbours.

nodes.label: Positional Encoding
nodes.desc: Adds order information so the model knows which token comes first, second or third.

nodes.label: RoPE
nodes.desc: Rotary position embeddings: encode position by rotating the query and key vectors.

nodes.label: Encoder-Decoder
nodes.desc: Encodes an input sequence and decodes an output sequence, in early models through one single vector.

nodes.label: Information Bottleneck
nodes.desc: One fixed vector cannot hold a long sentence, so early translation models lost detail.

nodes.label: Attention
nodes.desc: Lets every output step look at all the inputs and focus on the relevant ones.

nodes.label: Query, Key, Value
nodes.desc: A token asks a query, is matched against keys, and passes on the matching values.

nodes.label: Self-Attention
nodes.desc: Every token in a sequence attends to all other tokens of the same sequence.

nodes.label: Masked Attention
nodes.desc: Blocks looking at future tokens, so the model can only use the past when predicting.

nodes.label: Multi-Head Attention
nodes.desc: Several attention heads run in parallel, each learning a different kind of relation.

nodes.label: Grouped-Query Attention
nodes.desc: Heads share keys and values to save memory while keeping most of the quality.

nodes.label: Feed-Forward Network
nodes.desc: A small neural network applied to each token to transform what attention gathered.

nodes.label: Residual + Norm
nodes.desc: Skip connections and normalisation keep deep stacks of layers stable to train.

nodes.label: Transformer
nodes.desc: The architecture made of attention, feed-forward layers and residual connections; the basis of modern LLMs.

nodes.label: Large Language Model
nodes.desc: A very large Transformer trained to predict the next token on massive amounts of text.

nodes.label: Pretraining
nodes.desc: Learning general language ability by predicting the next token on enormous data.

nodes.label: Batching
nodes.desc: Processing many training examples at once to use the hardware efficiently.

nodes.label: GPU Compute
nodes.desc: Graphics processors perform the huge matrix multiplications of training and inference in parallel.

nodes.label: Number Precision
nodes.desc: Lower-precision formats such as bf16 save memory and time with little loss of accuracy.

nodes.label: Distributed Training
nodes.desc: Training is split across many GPUs, by data, by model parts or by layers.

nodes.label: Scaling Laws
nodes.desc: Loss falls predictably as model size, data and compute grow; this guides how to spend a budget.

nodes.label: In-Context Learning
nodes.desc: The model picks up a task from examples in the prompt, without changing its weights.

nodes.label: Supervised Fine-Tuning
nodes.desc: Further training on example instructions with good answers, to make the model helpful.

nodes.label: RLHF
nodes.desc: Uses human preference rankings to train a reward model, then tunes the LLM towards it.

nodes.label: DPO
nodes.desc: Learns directly from preference pairs, without a separate reward model or reinforcement learning.

nodes.label: Alignment
nodes.desc: Steering the model to be helpful, honest and safe according to human preferences.

nodes.label: Inference
nodes.desc: Running the trained model to generate text one token at a time.

nodes.label: Decoding
nodes.desc: The rule that picks the next token from the predicted probabilities.

nodes.label: Greedy Decoding
nodes.desc: Always picks the most likely token; deterministic but can become repetitive.

nodes.label: Temperature
nodes.desc: Sharpens or flattens the probabilities: low is safe and predictable, high is more creative.

nodes.label: Top-k Sampling
nodes.desc: Samples only among the k most likely tokens.

nodes.label: Top-p Sampling
nodes.desc: Samples from the smallest group of tokens whose probabilities add up to p.

nodes.label: RAG
nodes.desc: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: fetch relevant documents first, then let the LLM answer from them.

nodes.label: Hallucination
nodes.desc: Fluent but wrong or invented answers; grounding on retrieved facts reduces them.

nodes.label: Embedding Models
nodes.desc: Turn sentences or text chunks into vectors so that their meaning can be compared.

nodes.label: Chunking
nodes.desc: Splitting documents into pieces small enough to embed and retrieve.

nodes.label: Vector Store
nodes.desc: A database that stores embeddings and quickly finds the nearest ones.

nodes.label: ANN Search
nodes.desc: Approximate nearest-neighbour search trades a little accuracy for a lot of speed.

nodes.label: Dense Retrieval
nodes.desc: Finds passages by the vector similarity of their meaning.

nodes.label: BM25
nodes.desc: Classic keyword-based sparse retrieval that scores exact term matches.

nodes.label: Hybrid Retrieval
nodes.desc: Combines dense and sparse search to get the strengths of both.

nodes.label: Reciprocal Rank Fusion
nodes.desc: Merges several ranked result lists by summing 1 divided by (k plus rank) scores.

nodes.label: Evaluation
nodes.desc: Measuring quality with perplexity, task metrics, benchmarks and safety tests.

nodes.label: Benchmarks
nodes.desc: Standard test sets such as MMLU or HumanEval used to compare models.

nodes.label: BLEU, ROUGE, Pass@k
nodes.desc: Task metrics: BLEU and ROUGE compare text overlap, Pass@k checks whether generated code passes tests.
